title: Vitamin K2 MK7 Slows Artery Calcification (Phase 3 Trial)
description: When evaluating your of cardiovascular disease, the first question you should ask is not what your cholesterol is, but how much plaque is in your arteries. An actual measurement of plaque will beat a cholesterol level every time. And the most widely available and readily used measure is called the coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan. Data suggest that if you have a CAC score of zero, then irrespective of your LDL “bad” cholesterol, your risk of a cardiovascular event is low. This has come to be known as the “power of zero.” To that end, there’s a lot of interest in finding interventions that slow the progression of an artery calcification, since that’s thought to reduce cardiovascular risk. And one of the most popular and controversial supplements to potentially do so is vitamin K2 MK-7. Now, a major randomized, controlled phase 3 clinical trial just dropped a bombshell: Vitamin K2 MK-7 supplementation does indeed slow the progression of artery calcification. The finding sent ripples through the nutrition community, with vitamin K2 supplements flying off shelves at an alarming rate. But while these data are impressive and promising, there are critical nuances you need to know. What Is Vitamin K2 MK7? And How Does It work? First, let me describe what vitamin K2 MK-7 actually is. It’s a form of vitamin K2 that directs calcium into the places you want it, like your bones and your teeth, and away from the places that you don’t, such as your arteries. What makes the MK-7 form unique and thought to be superior is its long half-life, meaning it remains in your body for days rather than minutes or hours. And it’s thought to provide more sustained activation of vitamin K-dependent proteins than the vitamin K1 form, which you might get from something like a leafy green vegetable.

title: How to Use Gravity to Build Better Mitochondria
description: I had just gotten back from leg day when I sat down to read this paper. Halfway through, I stood up, put on a weighted vest, and kept reading. And by the time I finished, I realized that what I’d done in the gym that morning was a conversation. Every squat had sent a message to the quadrillions of tiny engines inside my muscles: Build more. Not just more muscle fibers, but more of the actual engine parts inside the mitochondria, the parts that produce energy. And that message travels through a molecular relay that starts with gravity itself. The first punchline, not to be missed: Your mitochondria feel gravity. How do we know? Well, when researchers sent cells to space, the mitochondria’s energy-producing machinery disappeared like the volume of spinach when you cook it. (The cooks among you know exactly what I mean.) That’s more than an esoteric bit of biology. It’s relevant to you every single day. But let me lay out (or stand up) what we’re going to learn today: How loading your skeleton can regulate your appetite. What long stretches of sitting do to metabolism, and a 2-minute habit that helps. A hidden way to lower glucose and insulin rises by 50 to 60% by using just 1% of your muscle mass. But first… to space! Mitochondria in Outer Space In a new study published in Nature Communications , researchers sent human cells to the International Space Station and performed a technique called “ribosome profiling,” which lets you measure protein synthesis in real time across the entire genome. They then compared cells cultured under normal gravity to cells cultured under microgravity. The finding: mitochondrial protein synthesis dropped dramatically under microgravity. But there’s a nuance we can’t miss.

title: My Plan to Never Get Alzheimer's Disease
description: When I was just 23 years old, I was handed a terrible verdict. I learned that I carried not just one copy but two copies of a genetic variant ( ApoE4/4 ) that dramatically increased my chances of developing Alzheimer’s disease, raising my risk by 12- to 15-fold. The great irony is that I received this news while I was pursuing my PhD studying neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. I knew exactly what this diagnosis meant, and I had already seen firsthand the devastation these diseases cause. My initial reaction was more than anxiety; it was terror. But I used that as fuel to dig deeper into the research. Now, seven years later, after earning a PhD in metabolism, completing medical school, and spending nearly a decade obsessively studying the science of brain health, I have something I didn’t have back then. I have tools. And most importantly, I have hope. In this letter, I’ll show you where the science stands, the specific tools I use , and the exciting future that’s coming next… *Author’s Note: A branching ecosystem of information A lot of what I write is dense, so I’m trying something a little more accessible with this letter. It’s self-contained, but also serves as a branching ecosystem of information. Wherever you see an asterisk (*), you’ll find a link to a separate 3,000- to 7,000-word deep dive for those who want to explore further. Lifestyle: A Clone Thought Experiment I want to begin with lifestyle. But rather than present you with a dry list, let me start with a thought experiment. Imagine I cloned myself, right down to the two copies of ApoE4 that supposedly sealed my brain’s fate. Then imagine those two versions of me walked off in opposite directions and lived out the next fifty years. In 50 years, one of us has Alzheimer’s.
